newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Scientists reject British plan to ease beef ban.
newsitem.headline: Scientists reject British plan to ease beef ban.

text.p: European Union veterinary scientists on Wednesday rejected a British bid to ease a worldwide ban on its beef exports by exempting herds certified free of mad cow disease.

"The proposal was not considered adequate in its present form because the scientific rationale and the information provided was insufficient," the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee said in a statement.

The scientists identified five weaknesses in the scheme proposed by Britain in February as a first step towards lifting a 15-month-old EU ban on British beef exports aimed at protecting the public against the human form of mad cow disease.
They suggested that if the British government corrected the weaknesses, the scheme could prove acceptable and the European Commission said the scheme should be amended.
"We hope the British government will take note and modify its proposal," said the Commission's food safety spokesman Filippo di Robilant.

The ban was imposed in March 1996 after Britain said that the fatal disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to humans who ate infected beef in the form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD).
The scientists said they were concerned firstly about the ability of the British certified herd scheme to identify and trace all cattle at risk to the fatal brain-wasting disease.
The scheme would initially have benefited Northern Irish herds because their movements have been tracked by computer records for the past eight years, unlike those in Scotland and England.
The committee urged a very cautious approach.
"The basis for any relaxation of export restrictions should be the identification of a "gold plated" standard...," they said in a report, listing criteria for herds, cattle and meat.
Herds must be of pure bred beef cattle, which have been isolated from other animals for more than six years and have never had any cases of BSE.
Cattle must be between six and 30 months old, born after August 1, 1996, and not offspring of animals that have had BSE.
Beef should be deboned because of the possible presence of infectious BSE agents in boned meat. Deboning of beef for export and for domestic consumption should be done separately.
In the statement, the scientists expressed concern about the tracing of live animals and of meat with and without bones.
They were also concerned about separate deboning of beef for export and domestic markets and of adequate disinfection.
Doubts were also raised about measures to prevent the mixing up of cattle, pig and poultry feed. Veterinary controls also needed to be clarified and realistic.
